top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B002) rests on a conceptually original general-equilibrium mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices and credit, so temporary shocks become large and persistent. It has about three decades of use in macro-finance, quantitative macro and policy modelling, and the 1997 founding paper has two authors, so there is no missing originator. Overlap with the 2022 prize is a judgment about distinct mechanisms (collateral feedback versus banks and runs), not a merit demerit. The empirical size of collateral amplification is less well identified than the theory's influence, and that is a real discount. P002 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, B012) is a close second: a mature measurement framework with real economic content (markups, substitution, welfare), but the omission of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin makes a three-name credit harder to defend. Both are clearly preferable to no award (P000), since each is a mature, defensible, narrowly creditable achievement.
recusal_note: No connection to Kiyotaki, Moore or the B012 names (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) appears in my profile. I am a frequent co-author and IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart, who support P001, and I co-authored a paper with Friberg. None of them is a candidate, and their agreement is not independent confirmation of merit. Macroeconomics is adjacent to B002. Disclosed without adjudication.
